The findings from the first co-design cycle can be divided into three main categories: predicted benefits based on procedure phases, potential robot behaviours, and risks and constraints. In this section, we outline the findings in each category; Section 4 shows how these findings were converted into technical system constraints. Procedure phases. The HCPs classified the predicted benefits of the robot-based intervention based on the three main phases of the IVI procedure. Before a pain-related procedure, HCPs stated that the ideal aim of the robot intervention is to provide emotional support and promote coping strategies. During a procedure, participants identified a change in the primary aim, i.e. the robot could behave as a distraction based on the child’s anxiety and engagement level and adapt to the child’s age-related preferences. Following the procedure, HCPs emphasised the importance of framing the medical procedure experience as positive for the child through positive reinforcement, rewards, and debriefing conversation by having the robot remain to support the child. Children and caregivers also highlighted the role of the robot-based intervention based on the three main phases. Caregivers emphasised the role of the robot during IVI procedure where it would cater distraction activities based on the child’s needs and preferences. Children highlighted the importance of the robot before and after the IVI procedure. They suggested the robot build rapport with them prior to the painful procedure by engaging in conversation and playing games, then focusing on positive reinforcement and de-briefing following the completion of the procedure.

Robot behaviours. HCPs felt that the proposed SAR should be equipped with a diverse range of actions to suit children’s needs, including encouraging dialogue, positive reinforcement phrases, humour, and cognitive behavioural strategies (e.g., breathing techniques, guided imagery, meditation). HCPs also felt that the proposed SAR should allow the user (i.e., child) to choose from a selection of options for distraction. In addition, the proposed SAR should also have the ability to estimate social signals and generate responsive social stimuli accordingly as children exhibit affective states (verbally, physically, and emotionally). Caregivers advocated for tailored language and distraction activities to match the child’s developmental level and recommended the robot have the ability to adapt to the child’s needs and respond in situationally appropriate ways. Children suggested physical enhancements for the robot including the colour of the robot, the voice of the robot, and preferred to robot remain in a standing position instead of sitting. Risks and constraints. HCP highlighted two main constraints on the system reliability. First, it must never speak over an HCP while information is being delivered; in other words, the system must maintain proper turn-taking between HCP and the robot. Second, the proposed SAR must not act inappropriately. This includes both emotional insensitivity (e.g., telling a joke when a child is crying), as well as situations where there is a lack of awareness of clinical deterioration (e.g., seizures, loss of consciousness). Caregivers were mainly concerned about the ability of the robot to respond in socially complex setting (such as the ED) and protecting their child’s privacy with regards to the robot videotaping and photographing the interaction. Children highlighted the technical failure of the SAR and its implications, such as losing control, as their main concern.

Rather than directly comparing outcomes with and without the robot, other studies have examined the impact of different robot behaviours. For example, Jibb et al. [16] compared user responses to a robot that used Cognitive Behavioural Therapy to one that used distraction: the children did not experience different levels of pain, but did feel less stress in the distraction condition. In addition to measuring the impact of the robot, Rossi et al. [25] found that adapting the robot’s behaviour to the child’s perceived anxiety level had a positive impact on distraction. Trost et al. [31] compared two versions of their robot, one that used empathic SAR and one that used distractive SAR: while they reported no significant difference on the mean scores of pain and distress, they do suggest that empathic SAR could be clinically more effective since children were more willing to receive the medical procedure in this condition. While most of the systems outlined above are designed to alleviate short-term pain and distress during a single procedure, stress reduction interventions involving social robots have also been explored in more long-term clinical contexts. For example, Ligthart et al. [18, 19] have developed a storytelling robot to support children in hospitals for a long term in an oncology ward. Although the robot has not yet been tested in a clinical context, the storytelling intervention has been shown to be engaging in a series of longitudinal studies involving primary-school children. Design practices such as co-design and user-centred design are well established in the HRI community [8]. These techniques balance the decision-making power between researchers and stakeholders, resulting in appropriate technology that also meets the needs of the target users [24]. These techniques are especially important when we want to approach real-world practices in complex scenarios such as the one considered here. All of this work takes place in the context of an increasing push in the HRI community to establish best practice standards to strengthen the evidence supporting the advantages of social robotics in different domains [34].

The use of the Zora robot was monitored and evaluated in 14 nursing care organizations (15 locations). The Zora robot, a Não robot with software, is designed as a social robot and used for pleasure and entertainment or to stimulate the physical activities of clients in residential care. In the ﬁrst year, the aim was to monitor and evaluate how the care robot is used in daily practice. In the second year, the focus was on evaluating whether the use of Zora by care professionals can be extended to more groups and other type of clients. Interviews, questionnaires and observations were used as instruments to reveal the progress in the use of the robot and to reveal the facilitators and barriers. Care professionals experienced several barriers in the use of the robot (e.g., start-up time and software failures). The opportunity they had to discuss their experience during project team meetings was seen as a facilitator in the project. Furthermore, they mentioned that the Zora robot had a positive inﬂuence on clients as it created added value for the care professionals in having fun at work. Keywords: long-term care facilities; older adults; gerontechnology

Working with a social robot like Zora is still in an experimental phase. Professionals have to be aware that things will not work perfectly immediately. Communication with staff and clients about this is crucial. Participating in such a project means acting as codesigners to enhance the technology innovation performance. In this phase, the Zora care robot showed added value when used in a rehabilitation setting to stimulate the movements of the clients while having fun. At the same, clients with psychogeriatric disorders might also beneﬁt from the Zora activities, especially those where the Zora robot is used in one-to-one situations. The students suggested some possible improvements based on their experiences and background. The suggestions they gave are practical and technical in nature. These suggestions have not been examined further. Think about how Zora can be used in the future for other activities. Use the function “word spotting” so Zora may respond (“listen”) better. Think about other ways of charging Zora, for example, with contactless charging; organizations will be able to use Zora for longer periods, for example, when they use Zora on a sheet with charging sensors, the robot can be charged while Zora is dancing. Use Artiﬁcial Intelligence Markup Language (AIML) to make it easier to have conversations. AIML works with programming patterns/scripts.

Based on the low-fidelity prototype, we developed a 3D-printed mid-fidelity prototype composed of three main parts (see Figure 2B): Base module: Designed to support mobility within the ED. It included two motorized wheels and two supports mounted on freewheels, an indoor robotic configuration that enables maneuverability and in-place turning, allowing the platform to move around the ED and enter the limited spaces beside patients’ beds. Mid-level module: Designed to increase the platform’s height and position its upper surface at a suitable level for blood tests. Top module: Designed to provide nurses with a work surface. Its surface is larger than the lower modules and includes a tray where nurses can safely place blood-test equipment rather than using the patient’s bed as an improvised surface. In addition, a robotic arm was positioned on the top of the platform to address the emotional challenges of the procedure by conveying social behaviors through non-verbal gestures. We chose a robotic arm because it can be used both for future functional applications and for performing gestures intended to enhance patients’ affective states. For all modules, we selected a rounded cubic form factor to evoke a friendlier, safer aesthetic than sharp-edged forms [4, 5, 14].

To address the emotional needs that emerged in the need study, we designed a set of non-verbal gestures for the robotic arm. The gesture design was based on well-established social cues known to enhance a sense of inclusion, security, and calmness [12, 13, 29, 38, 40, 49]. Based on human–human–robot interaction studies, the robotic arm was also designed to enhance interpersonal connection between the patient and the nurse. The resulting gestures were: Greeting: The arm greeted the patient and nurse by orienting its gripper towards both and performing three nodding movements. Attentiveness: The arm combined gaze-like orientation, leaning movements, and subtle nodding. Breathing: The arm oriented towards the patient while its upper part moved rhythmically to encourage slower, calmer breathing. Shared attention: The arm shifted its gaze-like orientation between nurse and patient to foster connection during the procedure. Goodbye: The arm performed three small nodding movements towards the patient and the nurse and folded inward. The understanding of the gestures was validated in a pilot study involving four patients and two nurses.

As technology becomes integrated into daily life, it offers promising opportunities to provide emotional support in healthcare contexts [3, 24]. Specifically, recent studies demonstrate the potential of robots to enhance patients’ affective states in the ED [1, 40]. Broader HRI research indicates that robots can support human affective states in various complex environments [9, 10, 40]. Importantly, these effects are not limited to highly sophisticated robots. Even simple robotic objects and machine-like robots can perform expressive gestures that are interpreted as consistent social cues [22, 29, 49]. Carefully designed interactions with such non-humanoid robots have been shown to enhance a sense of being acknowledged, safe, and cared for [29]. Beyond supporting individuals’ affective states, robots can also shape interactions between people [7, 13, 26, 27, 38]. When well designed, even simple peripheral robots can drastically enhance interactions between two humans without becoming another party in the interaction [13, 27, 38]. These findings suggest that in the ED, robots may also enhance moments of connection between patients and HCPs. However, the robot should fit within the complex healthcare context. To be accepted in this complex environment, it should also serve a functional purpose, even if minimal, and its appearance and behavior should be carefully designed. We present the design process of a robotic platform intended to support blood test experiences in the ED (see Figure 1). Building on the potential of robots to support patients’ affective states and patient–HCP interactions, we developed a mobile platform with a robotic arm that can perform gestures perceived as social cues signaling care, calming breathing, and attentiveness towards patients and nurses. The design process highlighted two needs: (1) providing practical assistance with managing blood test equipment; and (2) supporting the emotional needs of patients and nurses.

Relevant studies have evaluated robots that support affective states in hospitals and robots that enhance human–human interaction. Robots to support affective states in hospitals Previous research has indicated the social impact of robots in healthcare settings [1, 10, 15, 20, 28, 31, 40, 43, 47]. For example, Ali et al. [1] tested the impact of a humanoid robot on children treated in a pediatric ED. The robot provided supportive comments and demonstrated breathing exercises. Children and their parents reported significantly lower distress and greater satisfaction following the interaction. Rubin Kopelman et al. [40] showed that a much simpler robot performing minimal social gestures may also enhance patients’ experiences. They placed a non-humanoid, attentive robot in the adult ED waiting room at a public general hospital. Positioned in front of seated patients, the robotic object performed leaning, gaze and nodding gestures communicating attentiveness towards the patient. Findings showed that despite the robot’s simplicity and limited communication modalities, it positively influenced participants’ ED experience. We extend this line of work by examining whether a functional robot can be designed to support patients’ experiences during blood tests in the ED acute care area. Non-verbal robotic behavior to enhance H–H Interaction Various studies have indicated that non-verbal robotic behavior can shape human–human interactions [7, 16, 17, 23, 32, 36, 38, 41, 42, 44, 46, 48]. For example, Rifinski et al. [38] explored the effect of a peripheral non-humanoid robot on interpersonal evaluation during conversations. Participants engaged in a debate while a robotic object was positioned as a side participant. When the robot performed attentive gestures directed towards the speaker, participants evaluated their conversation partner more positively compared to those who interacted in the presence of a non-responsive robot. A more minimal robotic intervention was presented by Sadka et al. [41], who designed two robotic bar stools that could alter the body orientation of the people sitting on them. The stools turned strangers sitting on them towards each other. Their findings showed that this minimal movement facilitated positive social interactions and increased interpersonal communication. We extend this line of research by designing a functional robot intended to support patient–nurse interactions during a stressful healthcare procedure.

Participants also specified different physical characteristics for these robots. Robots for infotainment or preparation were often associated with using additional displays to either get the attention of more people in the waiting room. P3 suggested that “instead of just one monitor in the robot, put two or three so that if I put it in the middle of a room, anyone can see it”. P2 also recommended that they can also display more information for preparation and “show you a film of what the MRI will look like”. For a guide robot, participants specified height and speed requirements instead. A guide robot had to be tall enough to be visible so as not to cause accidents when moving in the crowded hospital environment as pointed out by P2. Also, the guide robot had to be fast enough when accompanying patients not to cause additional delays for the radiographer, and again P2 highlighted that “if [he] stand[s] there and ha[s] to wait three minutes for this guy to come and bring [him] the patient it becomes more of a disadvantage”. Our analysis also identified different robot capabilities that the participants either needed or wished for. Firstly, one of the underlying capabilities a robot would need in these roles is the ability to interact with multiple people simultaneously. In every scenario, the robot is always interacting at least with the parent and the child, and as pointed out by P3 the robot “ will always have two interlocutors at the same time, parent and child”. This becomes even more prevalent with the robot for infotainment, as highlighted by P2, which has to potentially interact with different families in the waiting room at the same time. The ability to speak different languages is also something the participants considered valuable. As children from various cultural backgrounds come into the hospital, it would make them feel more welcome to have a robot speak their native language. P4 mentioned that “languages like Arabic and Chinese would be very useful [..].The Chinese child is accompanied with instruction in his own language”.

This approach has been successfully used in HRI research, such as designing robots for elderly care [24], understanding perceptions of educational robots [23], or exploring robotic failures during robotic coaching [9]. In our focus group, we aim to answer our research questions, namely understand the hospital’s context in preparing children by identifying their needs (RQ1-a) and examining the current preparation process used by hospital staff to address them (RQ1-b); and explore how social robots could contribute to this process (RQ2). To analyze qualitative data from our focus group, we have used the Thematic Analysis (TA). This method has already been employed in HRI research when analysing qualitative data, with applications such as designing robot well-being coaches [7], [10], identifying moral considerations for social robots in education [23], and analyzing themes in dementia care data [17]. Given its proven effectiveness, TA is well-suited for our study.

secao: Findings > Humanoid robots are both likeable and scary
trecho: We discovered that the participants held ambivalent views on how humanoid robots are perceived. Some participants found robots to be kind and likeable, which, according to these participants, increases their sense of security. Others stated that they did not like robots that were too lifelike or had too many human traits. “[The robot] gives a trusting impression and it has a pleasant voice and a nice look. It is positive they have not tried to make it too human.” Several participants maintained that how individuals perceive robots will change over time as people become more accustomed to them. These participants revealed that the first time an individual encounters a robot in healthcare, the robot could be perceived as being scary, but that after the individual has become accustomed, robots “blend into the background”. These same participants stated that they believed robots would be considered a natural element in care in the future. Other participants expressed a completely divergent opinion, stating that robots were scary when they did not look human enough. Some participants found it difficult to understand what robots were saying and perceived robots’ speech as being unclear. These participants noted that they perceived robots’ voices to be unpleasant and stated that the robot they saw in the vignette was emotionless. One participant related that he found the physical presence of robots to be more frightening than when other “invisible” health technology services were used: “Perhaps I myself feel [the robot] to be more threatening than if it were somewhere in a cloud service assisting the nurse in his/her tasks, and not like it is, physically present”.

We found that some participants’ sense of security was improved in encounters with lifelike robots (cf., for example,33) Other researchers have also found that individuals prefer interacting with lifelike robots, because such are perceived to be more functional and more capable of engaging in activities than other, less lifelike robots (34,35) Some participants maintained that less lifelike robots were scary and that it could be difficult to understand what robots were saying because their speech was unclear. We therefore find that if individuals are to feel confident during interactions with robots, they must be able to understand what a robot is saying and be able to interpret the robot’s expression. This is in line with Wijk,23 who found that an individual’s experience of security is influenced by how clearly and easily they can interpret an environment. That the participants here expressed differing views on how lifelike robots should look can be compared to Wolpin and Stewart,36 who highlighted the importance of a patient-centered approach to technology, including that users are involved at an early stage in the design and evaluation process.

Following the video vignette, individual semi-structured interviews were conducted, during which the participants were asked to reflect on humanoid robots in healthcare. The interviews took place in a location chosen by each participant. The interviews were conducted in the form of a dialogue, and an interview guide (cf. 28) was used. The interview guide included the following questions, among others: How would it feel to be greeted by or taken care of by a humanoid robot? What are the advantages and disadvantages of humanoid robots? Would you feel safe and secure when meeting a humanoid robot (why/why not)? The questions included in the interview guide were supplemented with follow-up questions to deepen the participants’ responses. The interviews lasted between 25–60 minutes and were digitally recorded. The recordings were thereafter transcribed into text, resulting in 52 pages of text in total.

From the Godspeed Questionnaire, the user perception of the platform was evaluated (Figures 2E,F). Both groups rated the robot most favorably in the Animacy and Likeability categories. These two categories received median scores of 4.0 and 3.75 among Clinicians, respectively, while Perceived Intelligence and Perceived Safety obtained moderate median scores of 3.25. The Technician Staff provided similar positive perception ratings, with median scores of 4.0 on Likeability, 3.9 on Animacy, and 3.9 on Perceived Intelligence, although the latter showed a wide spread of individual variance ranging from 2.25 to 5.0. Among these categories, both groups showed that Anthropomorphism received the lowest evaluations, yielding median scores of 3.0 for Clinicians and 2.8 for Technicians, indicating that the platform was largely perceived as machine-like rather than human-like. Comparisons between the two groups revealed no significant differences across any of the Godspeed subscales (all p > 0.05). Regarding the remaining exploratory supplementary items (Figures 2G,H), both groups reported positive perceptions of interaction quality while teleoperating, with Clinicians reporting a mode score of 4.0 and Technicians a mode score of 3.0. Furthermore, both Clinicians and Technicians evaluated the platform’s suitability for interacting with children favorably, yielding mode scores of 3.0 and 5.0, respectively. Following this detailed subgroup comparison, data were further aggregated to evaluate the overall trends across all participants (Figure 3). The NASA-TLX analysis showed that teleoperation required mainly cognitive and effort loads (Figure 3A). Mental Demand and Effort had the greatest share in the total workload score, and the medians for these scales lay in the high workload spectrum (50–79). This interpretation is also supported by the percentage distribution showing that 69% and 61% of participants felt a high or very high level of mental and effort demand, respectively. In turn, Frustration received the lowest median score among the NASA-TLX dimensions (10–29).

The participants were asked to complete three standardized questionnaires immediately after using the platform. These instruments enable a rigorous evaluation of the perceived workload and mental fatigue, the usability of the robotic platform, and the perception of the robot’s features. Hence, we chose the NASA-TLX (Georgsson, 2020), the System Usability Scale (SUS) (Brooke, 1996), and the Godspeed Questionnaire Series (GQS) (Bartneck, 2023) questionnaires. Additionally, to capture contextual insights not covered by the standardized instruments, three ad hoc supplementary items were developed specifically for this study: • “How familiar are you with the virtual reality systems and/or gaming?” • “During the time when you were teleoperating the robot, did you feel that you could interact with the person you were talking to as you would like (communication, physical presence, etc.)?” • “How suitable do you consider the robot for interaction with a child?” These questions' purpose was to better understand if a participant’s prior experience with VR or gaming influenced their subjective perception and provide the level of the quality of HRI from both sides: the operator’s and the interaction partner’s point of view. It should be noted that these supplementary items are nonvalidated and were developed exclusively for exploratory purposes. Consequently, their results are interpreted purely as descriptive context to complement, rather than substitute for, the findings obtained from the standardized questionnaires.

Designing Machines That Feel More Human “Humanness” in robots emerges at the point where mechanical capability meets expressive, intentional-seeming behavior. An anthropomorphic form gives robots the physical affordances to act predictably, reason logically, and learn in nonlinear ways; paired with anticipatory gestures and affective cues, these capacities move them beyond automatic responses toward what looks like purposeful “caring”. Although robotics has not always meshed with nursing’s relational philosophy, contemporary “caring” robots demonstrate a kind of autonomy grounded in cognitive processing. Operationally, they render emotions through multimodal signal processing that mirrors the brain’s own electrical “eigenmodes” (Griffith & Hubbard Jr., 2021). This fusion of intelligence and emotion—whether implemented in biological neurons or neuromorphic chips—reproduces human-like experience and supports holistic behavior. robots equipped with authentic-looking caring abilities can embody aura” envisioned for nursing, positioning them to participate meaningfully in human care environments. Recent studies offer a coherent picture of how design and interaction cues shape human responses to social robots. Aligning anthropomorphic features with an appropriate communication style has been shown to increase user acceptance (Wu et al., 2024; Klüber & Onnasch, 2022), a finding that aligns with evidence on value configurational processing multimodal interaction capabilities (Sacino et al., 2022; Frederiksen, 2021). At the cognitive level, robots can convey internal states convincingly enough to elicit human-like gaze processing, as demonstrated in neural and behavioral studies (Li et al., 2023; Manzi et al., 2021; Tidoni et al., 2022). Nevertheless, designers must navigate wellknown pitfalls: the uncanny-valley effect and perspective-taking challenges can undermine user comfort (Wahn et al., 2023; Reuten et al., 2018), and overly engaging robots risk distracting users from primary tasks (Ghiglino et al., 2024; Urgen et al., 2020). Addressing these concerns, Erel et al. (2024) introduced the “Robot Social Influence” (RoSI) framework to guide ethically responsible interaction, while González- González et al. (2021) emphasized the pressing need to address privacy and accountability in real-world deployments. Together, this body of work charts a balanced path forward—using design insights to foster acceptance and engagement, while remaining vigilant about ethical, cognitive, and practical constraints.

Designing Machines That Feel More Human “Humanness” in robots emerges at the point where mechanical capability meets expressive, intentional-seeming behavior. An anthropomorphic form gives robots the physical affordances to act predictably, reason logically, and learn in nonlinear ways; paired with anticipatory gestures and affective cues, these capacities move them beyond automatic responses toward what looks like purposeful “caring”. Although robotics has not always meshed with nursing’s relational philosophy, contemporary “caring” robots demonstrate a kind of autonomy grounded in cognitive processing. Operationally, they render emotions through multimodal signal processing that mirrors the brain’s own electrical “eigenmodes” (Griffith & Hubbard Jr., 2021). This fusion of intelligence and emotion—whether implemented in biological neurons or neuromorphic chips—reproduces human-like experience and supports holistic behavior. robots equipped with authentic-looking caring abilities can embody aura” envisioned for nursing, positioning them to participate meaningfully in human care environments. Recent studies offer a coherent picture of how design and interaction cues shape human responses to social robots. Aligning anthropomorphic features with an appropriate communication style has been shown to increase user acceptance (Wu et al., 2024; Klüber & Onnasch, 2022), a finding that aligns with evidence on value configurational processing multimodal interaction capabilities (Sacino et al., 2022; Frederiksen, 2021). At the cognitive level, robots can convey internal states convincingly enough to elicit human-like gaze processing, as demonstrated in neural and behavioral studies (Li et al., 2023; Manzi et al., 2021; Tidoni et al., 2022). Nevertheless, designers must navigate wellknown pitfalls: the uncanny-valley effect and perspective-taking challenges can undermine user comfort (Wahn et al., 2023; Reuten et al., 2018), and overly engaging robots risk distracting users from primary tasks (Ghiglino et al., 2024; Urgen et al., 2020). Addressing these concerns, Erel et al. (2024) introduced the “Robot Social Influence” (RoSI) framework to guide ethically responsible interaction, while González- González et al. (2021) emphasized the pressing need to address privacy and accountability in real-world deployments. Together, this body of work charts a balanced path forward—using design insights to foster acceptance and engagement, while remaining vigilant about ethical, cognitive, and practical constraints.

secao: 4. DISCUSSION > 4.1. Representing Human “Intentionality” and “Empathy” in Robotics
trecho: adaptive technologies that learn through interactions (i.e., robots with contextual awareness) should enable nursing to foster richer, more meaningful interactions among caregivers, patients, and robotic assistants. By incorporating anthropomorphic features with emotional intelligence (EQ) and memory-based intelligence (IQ), these robots can engage in more sophisticated conversations and exhibit emotional responses, thereby embodying “compassion” in caregiving scenarios. This embodiment of “compassion” is rooted in “empathy,” as it involves the ability to understand and respond to information about the internal states of others, improving relational dynamics between humans and robots and fostering a more compassionate care environment. 4.1.1. “Empathy” Simulation Constraints in Robotics Park and Whang (2022) classify robot empathy into three ascending tiers. A “Type I Empathic Robot” is confined to a single domain, relies on one primary sensing channel, and can convey only rudimentary affective cues without deeper appraisal or modulation. A “Type II Empathic Robot” incorporates multiple sensor modalities and marries affective displays with limited cognitive appraisal, yet it remains bound to narrow task sets and delivers brief, contextspecific responses. A “Type III Empathic Robot” transcends these constraints by operating across domains, integrating numerous sensing channels, modulating both affective and cognitive processes, sustaining relationship awareness over time.

secao: 4. DISCUSSION > 4.1. Representing Human “Intentionality” and “Empathy” in Robotics
trecho: Park and Whang (2022) argue that genuine empathy in HRI depends on robots that can sense multimodal emotional cues, employ theory-based internal mechanisms—from motor mimicry to perspective taking—and deliver context-appropriate affective or cognitive responses that users recognize as “caring”. Their framework clarifies how perception, processing, and modulation jointly drive outcomes such as “trust,” “liking,” and “social presence,” and it offers a design roadmap that scales from simple scripted agents to sophisticated hybrid systems. Progress remains uneven: researchers still lack standardized metrics to gauge a robot’s empathic skill, domain-independent models that generalize across tasks, and long-term studies showing whether empathic behaviors endure over weeks or months. Complex mechanisms—classical conditioning, rich memory, and personality-aware tailoring—remain more conceptual than implemented, and the influence of robot form factors on empathy perception is only lightly explored. Closing these research gaps calls for long-term studies, shared evaluation standards, and hybrid systems that merge theoretical models with data-driven algorithms; together, these steps can turn social robots from lab prototypes into reliable, empathic partners that function effectively in real-world settings.

Our theme supporting this construct was anthropomorphism, and the related theme of gendering/objectifying (Table I). Evidence of anthropomorphizing suggests participants attributed feelings to robots, even empathising with devices, “are you having a bad day? [Miro].” This supports participants feeling they were in the company of a social entity [17], as would participant tendency towards gendering robots, “she must be a girl with those eyelashes [Paro].” There were 89 occasions of gendering, compared to 35 counts of objectifying. Viewing the robots as objects could provide evidence against Social Presence, whilst projecting a gender could suggest the robot is perceived as a being rather than a thing [23], therefore capable of social presence. Interestingly, all evidence for Social Presence was directed towards SAR with anthropomorphic or biomorphic design (Pepper, Miro, Paro), whilst Padbot received no evidence for anthropomorphism or gendering.

A further consideration noted was for improved voice recognition and accent interpretation, with issues raised regarding conversational fluency, accent interpretation and noisy environments. Pending advancements in voice recognition software, a potential solution is using other human-robot interfaces. Successful human-robot interaction would be key in ensuring usefulness of robots in H&SC. While technical issues appeared endearing to participants here, issues faced during real-world implementation would likely cause frustration. Another considerations likely to become relevant in real-world H&SC settings is improved mobility for uneven floors, carpets and rugs, particularly for SAR to be implemented across a range of H&SC contexts. Design considerations to account for varied and uneven floor surfaces seems a feasible alteration to improve acceptability specifically for this sector. This study also identified importance of better perceived robustness of devices, to alleviate fear of damage. Devices might also aim for a long battery life or autonomous charging, as suggested by our stakeholders, to remove potential distress of a device ‘dying.’ Autonomous charging may also support ease of use. Generally, our evidence supports ease of use for the robots demonstrated, particularly for Paro and Miro, however some concern was shown towards usability of Pepper, with the quantity of options on the tablet appearing overwhelming for some. Options could be streamlined on app-based SAR dependant on intended setting to improve perceived ease of use. Improvements in verbal communication would also reduce the need for tablet based interaction with multiple apps.

Different types of social robotic interventions were identified. Six of the studies used some type of humanoid robot (Kasimoglu et al. 2023, 2020; Franconi et al. 2023; Topçu et al. 2023; Lee‐Krueger et al. 2021; Beraldo et al. 2019), whereas one study used an interactive robotic ride‐on car (Lapedriza et al. 2024). It was the only robot designed and customised by the research team, whereas the others were pre‐existing models. All robots included in the reviewed studies were hardshelled designs; none were reported as having soft‐body construction. Detailed features of the robots are shown in Table 5. Four studies tested their robotic interventions preoperatively; either while the paediatric patients were waiting for their surgery (Lapedriza et al. 2024; Lee‐Krueger et al. 2021) or up until the sedation or anaesthesia was induced (Franconi et al. 2023; Beraldo et al. 2019). Two of the studies tested their robotic interventions during the procedures (dental treatment) (Kasimoglu et al. 2023, 2020) and one conducted the intervention postoperatively (Topçu et al. 2023). The studies had slightly different settings or contexts in which they were testing the robotic interventions. Two of the studies included elements of preoperative care for minor surgeries or procedures (Franconi et al. 2023; Beraldo et al. 2019), and two studies tested the interventions during paediatric dental treatments (Kasimoglu et al. 2023, 2020). One study was done in a setting of a preoperative transport for paediatric surgeries (Lapedriza et al. 2024), and one tested a robotic intervention in a setting for IV induction for elective surgeries (Lee‐Krueger et al. 2021). One study tested the robotic intervention for post‐operative mobilisation after minor surgery (Topçu et al. 2023). Most of the studies compared the interventions with standard care (Lapedriza et al. 2024; Franconi et al. 2023; Kasimoglu et al. 2023, 2020; Topçu et al. 2023; Lee‐Krueger et al. 2021). However, one study compared two different robotic interventions to each other, without a control (Beraldo et al. 2019).

This review examined social robotic interventions aimed at reducing children's anxiety, pain, fear and stress in perioperative nursing. The interventions varied from interactive humanoid robots providing emotional support to task‐oriented robots guiding children through medical procedures. Evidence showed that these robots were particularly effective in reducing postoperative anxiety through engaging interactions. However, findings related to pain, fear and stress were more limited. Overall, social robots appear to be promising tools in paediatric perioperative care, but further research is needed to identify the most effective interventions for various emotional and physiological outcomes. Although the available data are still scant, social robots appear to offer valuable distraction techniques, an approach that has increasingly been acknowledged as beneficial in paediatric healthcare settings (Pan et al. 2024; Dawe et al. 2019). The interventions included four RCTs and three quasi‐experimental studies featuring interactive humanoid robots, or in one case, a ride‐on robotic car (Lapedriza et al. 2024). Across these studies, the robots interacted with children in various ways. Some interventions provided mere distraction, such as playing, singing or dancing, whereas others featured more immersive engagement with cognitive‐behavioural strategies, such as active engagement, education and teaching of coping strategies during stressful medical procedures. These deeper level interactions appear to be an important differentiator: prior research suggests that passive distraction may be less engaging and less effective than emotionally immersive interventions (Ferraz‐Torres et al. 2022; Trost et al. 2020). However, in this review, both distraction and cognitive‐behavioural strategies showed positive effects in some of the studies, although the findings were not consistent across all.

All the studies provided some form of social robotic distraction for paediatric patients during procedures. Most of them also provided emotional support or encouragement (Franconi et al. 2023; Kasimoglu et al. 2023; Topçu et al. 2023; Lee‐Krueger et al. 2021; Beraldo et al. 2019). The used distraction methods included music or sounds (Lapedriza et al. 2024; Franconi et al. 2023; Topçu et al. 2023; Kasimoglu et al. 2020), discussion and play (Franconi et al. 2023; Beraldo et al. 2019), dancing (Franconi et al. 2023), lights and animation (Lapedriza et al. 2024; Kasimoglu et al. 2020) as well as body movements (Topçu et al. 2023) with facial expressions (Kasimoglu et al. 2023, 2020). In addition, three studies included more interactive, robotic functions with cognitive‐behavioural strategies to help manage children's and adolescents' perioperative negative emotions. In one study, the robot provided basic educational preparation and encouragement for the children and simulated mask anaesthesia during induction (Franconi et al. 2023). In one study, the robot accompanied its users during postoperative mobilisation (Topçu et al. 2023), whereas in another one, the robot guided deep breathing exercises and provided interactive encouragement as a coping strategy for children during a stressful procedure (Lee‐Krueger et al. 2021).

The data were extracted using a modified data extraction template (Centre for Reviews and Dissemination 2009), including key variables such as study characteristics, intervention and control descriptions, outcome measures, measurement instruments, time points, statistical methods and main findings. Two reviewers independently extracted data from all eligible studies. The extraction process covered the PICOS framework and included both study design details and outcome data. The characteristics of the studies included (Table 4) were charted using predefined variables: first author, year of publication, study context and population (including age, size and eligibility criteria), study design, type and content of intervention, outcome measures (e.g., anxiety, pain, fear, stress), time points and data collection methods. The findings were recorded for both interventions and control groups. Moreover, study aims and descriptions of robots used in the interventions were charted separately (Table 5). After independent extraction, the reviewers compared their findings and resolved discrepancies through discussion. Descriptions of the robots used in the interventions. In this review, anxiety was identified as the primary outcome, as it was the most commonly reported and central outcome in evaluating the effects of social robots for children and adolescents in perioperative nursing. The secondary outcomes were defined as pain, fear and stress. In addition to the predefined protocol, one other outcome clearly related to the topic (pulse) was found when examining the studies. Where available, the extracted data included quantitative results such as means, standard deviations, p‐values and statistical comparisons.

An overview of the software and hardware components described in this section is shown in Fig. 2. The trials were carried out with NAO, a 58 cm tall humanoid robot with 25 degrees-of-freedom manufactured by Aldebaran. NAO is equipped with two cameras, an array of microphones as well as several proximity sensors. It is able to stand and walk on its own. NAO has a non-threatening appearance due to its small size and cartoon-like features. Furthermore it has successfully been deployed in many social robotics trials [2,25]. Aldebaran provides a library called NAOqi for developers to control NAO’s behaviour. We used two NAOs during trials, though only one at a time. Having two robots allowed us to run trials continuously withouttheriskofemptybatteriesoroverheatingrobotjoints. NAO stood on top of a rolling table with its feet anchored to the table by velcro, this way the 58 cm tall robot was able to interact with patients face to face. This set-up also had the advantage of allowing us to move the robot from bed to bed quickly. The ﬂexibility lost by anchoring the robot feet was balanced with the extra safety of stopping the robot from falling on the patient in the event the motors failed. We used Wi-Fi to communicate between the robot and the tablet-PC which ran our custom remote operator interface (Fig. 2e). The robot (Fig. 2a) received motor and speech commands from the remote operator interface and transmitted video from its top camera as well as audio from its front microphone. However, the relatively low-bandwidth and variable latency of Wi-Fi communication meant that the sound was noisy with occasional fragments of sound missing and that the camera resolution was limited to 160 × 120 pixels.

Controls for rapidly adjusting NAO’s speaking volume in the remote operator interface were found to be important very early on, as was the ability to trigger stored behaviours on the robot. Finally, we programmed the interface so that if the remote operator clicked anywhere on the view of NAO’s camera, NAO would move the head toward that point. This allowed the operator to ensure NAO was looking at the patients even if they shifted positions. Our remote operator interface also was executed on the tablet-PC which helped make the interaction more responsive as the operator could simply touch the desired behaviour, speech ﬁller or gaze position. This remote operator interface is an instantiation of what in the literature is known as Wizard of Oz [18]. ROS has the ability to save all the information that it transmits to a log ﬁle (Fig. 2b). During trials we recorded interaction aspects such as robot’s camera view and the robot activities into the log ﬁles. These were later used for analysis purposes. Putting all these components together allowed us to program NAO so it was able to perform the following actions to socialise with patients: – Read the news (pre-fetched on the morning). – Demonstrate arm ﬂexing and stretching exercises and then request that the patient repeats them. – Perform two dances: one was Tai chi inspired and relax- ing; the other was more energetic and based upon the work of Ros et al. [23]. Furthermore, NAO would ask some of the following questions to patients as a means to start a conversation: – How are you? Or, alternatively, are you comfortable? – How is your family?

Recent research on social robots in diabetes management for children can be categorized into two main areas: diabetes management systems and diabetes education systems. This section critically examines the existing literature, highlighting the key findings, methodologies, and gaps in the current knowledge. First, the diabetes management systems are considered: The majority of studies have focused on using robots for diabetes management. Al-Taee et al. [10] investigated the use of NAO robots with 22 participants, reporting the high acceptability of the robot solution. This was further corroborated by another study [11] with a larger sample size of 37, which found an overall acceptability of 86.7%. These studies suggest that children are generally receptive to robot-assisted diabetes management. Alhmiedat and Alotaibi [12] explored a different platform, the SARA robot, with a small sample of five participants. Despite the limited sample size, they reported a reasonable acceptance rate of 82.2%, indicating that various simple robot platforms may be suitable for this purpose. Several studies utilized the NAO robot platform for different aspects of diabetes management. Blanson Henkemans et al. [13] reported an increase in diabetes knowledge among 27 participants. Van Der Drift et al. [14] found that children shared more personal experiences in their diaries when interacting with the NAO robot, albeit with a small sample size of six. These studies suggest that robot interaction may enhance engagement and knowledge retention. Cañamero and Lewis [15] and Kruijff-Korbayová et al. [16] both used NAO robots with sample sizes of 17 and 20, respectively, reporting positive outcomes in terms of social interaction and children’s interest in engaging with the robot. This indicates that robots can serve as effective companions in diabetes management.

SOLUTION 1. The social robot helps to break daily routine. 2. It mediates between kids and doctors. 3. It explains medical procedures and remember past events. 4. It withstands cleaning and sanitizing procedures. 5. It requires some help from the patient for moving. According to the well-known User-Centered Design (UCD) approach, several prototypes have been made to better assess user interaction and improve the final goals. The first prototype was made in polystyrene and clay to estimate proportions and size. Subsequently, a 3D printed model and a silicone sock helped to evaluate embodiment and appearance. The working prototype aided to test user interaction adopting an embedded Arduino Mega board that controlled two LCDs for the eyes of the robot, two speakers for its voice while three LEDs were adopted to simulate facial expressions. It also included 4 touch sensors, each one triggering a different reaction. Edu’s working prototype required three months of iterative processes focusing on user tests and improvements. Figure 1 depicts outcomes of the design process from the initial model until the final prototype. The term care robotics as used in this paper encompasses all machines that operate partly or fully autonomously performing care-related activities for people with physical and/or mental handicaps. These handicaps are related to age and/or health-related restrictions. Among others care robots are meant to simplify tasks of the daily life for aged and/or otherwise handicapped people. Such highly specialized machines shall increase the quality of life of their users by giving them more autonomy [1], by protecting them and/or by performing certain tasks with a certain quality standard (for example serving medication, drinks or food). Different types of care robotics have already been developed. The Care-O-Bot is a first example [2]. Already in its third generation this autonomously operating device is being developed by the Fraunhofer Institute for Manufacturing Engineering and Automation (IPA), Germany. The third generation has a grappler in the back and a tray in the front. It can detect obstacles, move around and avoid them. Having the appearance of a robotic “butler” this machine fulfills a repertoire of transporting functions. For instance, it delivers water to residents in senior homes or hospitals. The care robot identifies, approaches and talks to its “customers”. It documents its work and allows doctors and care takers to analysis that data (e.g. to verify whether patients have consumed sufficient water over a day). A very different type of a care robot is Paro, a robotic baby seal that has been developed for patients suffering from dementia. Developed by Takanori Shibata at the National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology (AIST) in Japan, Paro is equipped with two microphones and several sensors to detect light, sound and other environmental stimuli. On an emotional level Paro interacts with patients through movements of its fins and eyes [3]. Research about the effects of Paro use in therapeutic treatments shows that it has a stimulating as well as a calming effect on the patients, facilitating discussions and interactions among dementia patients and influences the affectionate behavior of those positively when turned on [3]. Paro is the first commercially available care robot.

Due to the expected growth for care-robots in the future and the need for dedicated care-robot research this paper seeks to provide a comprehensive evaluation of the field contributing answers to the following two questions: 1. Which organizations and individuals in which countries have been and are active in related research and development? 2. How has related research and development emerged with regard to activity focus, intensity levels and cooperation? The remainder of the paper is divided into four sections. Following the brief introduction to care robotics, we have presented our research questions. The next section introduces our methodological approach. Results of bibliographic and network analyses are presented in the third section. The fourth section discusses the results reflecting upon both research questions and suggests for further research.

secao: 5 Discussion > 5.1 Meeting Young Adults' Needs—Through Orientation, Working and Termination Phases
trecho: According to previous research in health care (Coeckelbergh et al. 2016; Poulsen et al. 2018; Christoforakos et al. 2021), the most important thing in communication among healthcare is an efficient technique, being direct with the patient. Gestures or body language that express the robot's confidence increase trust (Townsend and MajidiRad 2022). The young adults expressed that the robot's ability to take initiative in a friendly manner was important to reduce repetitive uncertainty and build trust. For example, beginning the conversation with a friendly greeting reduces uncertainty and builds trust. The findings from this study can also be discussed in light of a similar study (Gasteiger et al. 2020) that examined the role of greeting behaviour in human‐robot interaction in delivering medications. The findings suggest that while presence (whether virtual or physical) is important, it is not just the physicality of the robot but how it engages emotionally and socially with the user that matters. Also, previous research (Rosenberg et al. 2024) shows concerns about the robot's lack of body language, which was seen as problematic as it might limit its ability to interpret nonverbal cues. This study extends these findings, as young adults emphasised the importance of the robot to communicate in a friendly and socially appropriate manner, indicating that both verbal and nonverbal communication play a key role in building rapport and trust in Human‐Robot Interaction.

Data were analysed using deductive, reflexive thematic analysis (Braun and Clarke 2022), focusing on broad thematic patterns across all data from a constructivist perspective. Reflexive thematic analysis is particularly suited for studies like this due to its flexibility and accessibility (Braun and Clarke 2022, p. 261). The deductive analysis was carried out manually, concentrating on exploring the realities and meanings of the needs in relation to social robots raised by the participants. The analysis process began by reviewing the interviews multiple times and an initial analysis of the interview transcripts by code categorisation was conducted by three of the authors (M.A., S.H., L.E.). The same authors collaborated to enhance the validity and reliability. Initial themes put forward by the first author (M.A.) were finalised and confirmed as themes at the end of the analysis process through discussions, including all the researchers in the team (M.A., S.R., S.H., M.W., A.L., L.E.). The themes developed from the data content were shaped by the theoretical framework provided by Peplau (1952). After reviewing the codes and dataset, the authors identified three main themes related to participants' needs in relation to social robots. Each theme is expressed through Peplau's interpersonal relation theory, symbolising the dynamic and evolving nature of human‐robot relations. Illustrative participant quotes help highlight the driving motives behind their willingness to build a relationship with the robot in medication counselling.

The appearance of the robot was also discussed. The small size and ‘childish’ appearance of the NAO robot were reported as limitations, with the lack of facial expressions creating problems in conveying empathy. Although small robots such as NAO and Paro have already been used in healthcare settings [42], larger robots such as Pepper [43] or AIRSTAR (LG) may be more suitable. This is because they are more difficult to push over and are more mobile and accessible using the tablet/touchscreen, which could display a map, text or graphics. However, Pepper’s facial expres sions are similar to NAO’s, which are quite limited. This can be problematic as facial expressions are an important healthcare communication behavior [23]. Interestingly, some participants also wanted the robot to look like a doctor or nurse. This may feed into expec tations regarding stereotypes. Previous research has shown that users prefer robots when they match the (stereotyped) gender-occupational role. For example, a healthcare robot was rated more positively by 164 participants when it was female-gendered and a security robot was better rated when it was male-gendered [44].

The audio for all videos was developed on Amazon Polly, using prosodic changes (pitch, volume, and rate/speed) to convey positive, negative, and neutral sentiment (feeling). For example, positive speech was higher pitched, slightly faster, and louder than non-empathetic responses (see Sup plementary file). Sentiment rather than emotion was used, as this can be easier for participants to detect [28]. The Austra lian ‘Nicole’ voice was used, given that people prefer robots to sound like themselves, thus similar accents should be used [29–31]. The New Zealand accent was not available. Throughout all interactions, NAO was relational by referring to the patient by their name and referring to itself (as a social entity). It also gave options to visitors, such as whether they would like to engage in the interaction (e.g., Do you want me to entertain you?) or what response they would like (e.g., Do you want to hear a joke or watch me dance?). Humor was used in the entertainment task by offering to making jokes and showing a dance. The responses were simple and universally relatable, to ensure they appeal to a diverse audience. Relational gestures included greeting the patient by waving (see Fig. 1), beckoning when asking them to come closer and pointing and gazing in a direction when giving directions. Further detail on the prosodic changes and text used, as well as the gestures and social skills can be found in the Supplementary file.

This work contributes to an ongoing research program that seeks to develop empathetic social robots in health care. The model of Robot-Patient Communication [20] theorizes that robots should convey affective empathy in order to optimize patient outcomes. In this model, clinical empathy is described as being able to understand a patient’s symptoms, feelings and perspectives, and communicate this understanding to the patient, check this understanding, and act on this in a therapeutic way. The model describes both verbal and non-verbal ways to convey empathy, and a series of studies have systematically tested several behaviors in the model. The previous work has included a randomized controlled trial with 181 participants to examine the effect of robot attentional behaviors (self-disclosure, voice pitch and leaning forward) on user perceptions and behaviors in a healthcare scenario [21]. Self-disclosure and leaning forward were found to increase engagement and attention, but no significant effects were found for the voice pitch changes. A repeated measures study with 40 participants and the EveR-4 android robot explored the effects of smil ing and use of the participant’s first name by a healthcare receptionist robot [14]. This work found that smiling and the use of first names had positive effects on perceptions of a robot’s personality. A third study examined the use of humor by a healthcare robot (EveR-4) with 91 participants [22]. The study found that the humorous robot was perceived as having significantly more empathy and a more sociable personality than a non-humorous robot. Participants were also more likely to laugh when interacting with the humor ous robot. In a fourth study, verbal empathy statements by a healthcare robot were shown to increase perceived robot empathy, trust, and satisfaction, although head nodding did not have any significant effects on outcomes. This work contributes to our knowledge of which behaviors to build into healthcare robots to convey clinical empathy and opti mize outcomes, but more research is required, especially on voice pitch, eye gaze, gestures, and interruptions [23].

The survey was hosted on secure site Qualtrics, which par ticipants accessed using a link. Prior to recruitment, the survey was tested by a 33-year-old female external to the research team, for readability and clarity. Before starting the survey, participants read an informa tion sheet and give consent on Qualtrics. The survey was expected to take up to 15 min to complete. At the end of the survey, participants were able to elect to receive a lay summary of the findings and enter the draw to win one of three $100 (NZD) shopping vouchers. This incentive was expected to encourage the completion of the survey, to mini mize the number of incomplete responses. Demographic data were collected, including gender, age, ethnicity, and the highest level of educational attainment. Previous experience with robots was measured as follow ing: none; a little (e.g., have seen photos or videos of them); a moderate amount (e.g., have used them) or a lot (e.g., work with them, studied robotics or similar, own a robot). Expe rience with hospitals was also measured: none (e.g., have never been to hospital); a little (e.g., attend very rarely); a moderate amount (e.g., attend sometimes) or a lot (e.g., work there; frequently attend as a visitor, patient, or support person). Attitudes towards robots were assessed using the validated 14-item Negative Attitudes Towards Robots Scale [27]. Three subscales were used: the 3-item Negative Atti tudes toward Emotions in Interaction with Robots (range 3–15), the five-item Negative Attitudes toward Social Influ ence of Robots (range 5–25) and the six-item Negative Atti tudes toward Situations and Interactions with Robots (range 6–30) [27]. Higher scores indicate more negative attitudes.

Regarding the patients, more than half of them interacted with the robot which points to the acceptance of the robot (RQ3). However, there were significant differences in robot evaluation between patients and medical staff concerning appreciation of the robot’s presence in the office and robot liking which were both higher for the staff. This finding may be explained by the design process. In user-centered design, it is important to include each representative user to understand all the representative needs [14]. While we involved the medical staff in the design of the prototype, the stakeholder group of patients was yet not included. This might explain the differences in robot evaluation obtained in our field study. Further, the age difference between staff and patients (staff’s mean age M = 22.33, patients’ mean age M = 41.64) indicates a potential variance in technological exposure and acceptance and could also be one possible reason for the different perception of the robot. For example, in a project by Wilson et al. [15] on designing a custom application for an organization, mainly seniors with high knowledge and experience were included as users, while the needs of temporary staff or juniors were disregarded, leading to a refusal to use the new system among these groups. Further explanations can be derived from the interviews. As one of the staff members mentioned, they needed time to get used to the new technology of social robots. While the employees took part in the interviews at the end of the 10day-long intervention, patients answered the questionnaires after a short time of interacting with the robot. This speaks rather for a mere exposure effect (see e.g., [16]) than for a novelty effect (see e.g., [17]). Another explanation may be the work relief perceived by the employees as reported from the interviews, which outweighed the entertaining aspect of the robot for the patients. The advantages of the social robot in the medical office might have been greater for the staff than for the patients, resulting in a better evaluation of the social robot from the personnel.

For our study, we chose the Pepper robot since its tablet allows to visually display information. secao: V. FIELD STUDY > A. Methods and Measures
trecho: Using a multi-methods approach, we conducted semistructured interviews with the medical staff and utilized questionnaires to capture patients’ as well as staff’s perceptions of the robot to gain insights into how the robot is perceived by both stakeholders. 1) Questionnaire Data: The questionnaire comprised informed consent, demographic data, actual interaction with the robot (yes/no), open-ended comments, and three questions on the robot which are displayed in Table I. The questionnaire was filled out by patients and medical staff. 2) Interviews: We conducted semi-structured interviews with the medical staff working on the days during our study. First, we asked about the general acceptance of the robot, as well as any disturbing or annoying features. Then the staff were asked about future activities and areas of application of the robot in the medical practice (e.g., ”Should Paula support you with your work?” or ”Would you like to have the robot carry out the entire registration process or only parts of it?). Afterward, there were questions about the influence of the robot on the staff’s work, e.g., ”Do you feel restricted in your work by the robot?”. Finally, there was a question about the common future in the cooperation between humans and robots. Follow-up questions were asked when appropriate.

Another limitation of our study is that the impressions of the patient were formed in the absence of any other information about the patient. In real-life scenarios, even for very short, first-time interactions, people give off an abundance of signals about who they are (age, gender, ethnic group, and social class) and research has shown that humans are able to form impressions extraordinarily fast [49]. It is therefore likely that the robot’s effect on people’s impression might be greatly modulated by the information conveyed by the patient herself. For example, people might hold different beliefs to start with in terms of how much agency someone should have over their own treatment based on whether they are an older adult versus a young adult versus a child. In our vignettes, people’s characteristics were left completely to the participant’s imagination, and some might have formed very vivid images of the patient whereas others less so. Similarly, the robot characteristics were left to the imagination of the participants, which might have contributed to how the robot was perceived. The contributions of various characteristics to the robot perception are likely mixed. For example, the findings of Fan et al [43] suggest that some characteristics are very resistant to changes in the perception of EI in robots: the robot’s voice and gestures did not have an influence on people’s ratings of the robot’s EI, the authors finding no differences between video, audio, or text vignettes. It seems that what the robot says is the single most important factor in how emotionally intelligent the robot is perceived. However, another study [44] found that the robot assigned gender (indicated through name), in addition to what the robot said influenced how emotionally intelligent the robot was perceived to be.

To our knowledge, this is the first investigation that probed the potential influences of assistive robots on how patients are judged by others. By simply varying the way the robot gives a treatment progress report (manipulating the language used, but not the facts conveyed), the robot makes a significant difference to the extent to which the patient is thought of as likable, self-disciplined, competent, and having a positive attitude as opposed to being hostile, disruptive, and disorganized. People take cues from the robot, and when the robot uses a patient-centered language that indicates respect for the patient’s agency, as opposed to a task-centered language that focuses on the treatment benchmarks, people form a more positive impression of the patient. It is remarkable that robots are able to have this effect given that their language output is scripted and certainly does not come with the emotional connotations that a person’s choice of language would have. A robot’s behavior is not connected to beliefs and attitudes in the same way a human’s behavior is, yet our findings suggest that we inadvertently let our perceptions and impressions of others be guided by the robot’s actions. This can be seen both as having cautionary implications for the field of human-robot interaction but also as an opportunity for the field: if robots can have an influence on how we think of others, then perhaps they can be used for improving relationships in the health care setting and beyond.

secao: Methods > Measures > Perceptions of Robot Emotional Intelligence
trecho: We used a 24-item questionnaire based on a measure developed by Caruso and Salovey [45] and previously used by Fan et al. [43] to measure perceptions of EI in robots. Items referred to emotion perception (eg, “Knows why people feel the way they do”), understanding (eg, “Considerate of others’ feelings”), and management (eg, “Creates positive moods in people”) capacities and participants indicated, on a 5-point Likert scale, how much each statement described the robot in the vignette from 0=not at all to 4=very much so (Cronbach alpha=.96). We averaged the scores from all the items for each participant.
